instructions:
## The project being researched

An XGBoost "virtual sensor" for Iowa stream nitrate: predict at locations with NO physical sensor, using only weather + land-use data. Two targets:
- REGRESSION: daily-max nitrate concentration (mg/L)
- CLASSIFICATION (the primary one): binary `violation` = daily max >= 10 mg/L, base rate 0.263

~85 sensor sites, 160,074 site-days, 2008-2026. Each site has a delineated upstream drainage basin. Features are aggregated over basin cells in distance buckets from the outlet.

## THE DEPLOYMENT TARGET - judge every recommendation against this
The shipped product takes an ARBITRARY MAP PIN anywhere in Iowa, delineates its upstream basin on the fly via USGS NLDI, builds features from weather and land use alone, and predicts daily violation probability. There is NO nitrate history at the target location, NO discharge gauge there, and NO guarantee of a monitored neighbor upstream. Any method that requires the target site's own observations, or requires a gauged upstream site, DOES NOT WORK for this product - it may still be useful for other purposes, but that limitation must be stated explicitly and prominently.

## Current honest performance (leave-one-basin-family-out, LOFO)
- CLF: AUC 0.820, PR-AUC 0.634 (2.41x lift over base rate), recall 0.524 at 10% false-alarm rate, MCC 0.466, Brier 0.137
- REG: R2 0.328, RMSE 4.36 mg/L
- Deployed at beta=2: recall 0.864, but 59% of alarms are false

## THE CENTRAL PROBLEM: the model cannot rank sites
- within_r2 0.42 vs between_r2 0.21
- macro_auc 0.90 vs between_rate_r2 0.24
The project's own summary: "a good timer, a mediocre site-ranker." It captures WHEN nitrate rises at a given site, but fails at the ABSOLUTE LEVEL of an unseen basin. Essentially all remaining headroom is in the between-site term.

## CRITICAL SAMPLE-SIZE CONSTRAINT
The ~85 sites collapse to only 19 INDEPENDENT BASIN FAMILIES under the leak-safe CV (sites whose basins nest and whose records overlap in time are grouped). So learning a site's absolute level is a regression with roughly 19 effective independent units, NOT 160k rows. Any method whose published gains come from hundreds of catchments (e.g. CAMELS with 531-671 basins) must be explicitly flagged as possibly infeasible here.

## Current features (68 for CLF)
9 weather variables x 3 distance buckets (SAME-DAY SCALARS ONLY), 8 CDL crop classes x 3 buckets, 2 nitrogen-surplus x 3 buckets, doy_sin/doy_cos, 4 cross-site nitrate lags (rest_of_state_nitrate_lag1/2/3/5), 5 static (lat, lon, log_basin_area, mean_dist_to_sensor, max_dist_to_sensor).
Top features by permutation importance: rest_of_state_nitrate_lag1, lon, lat, doy_sin, fuel_moisture_1000h. BOTTOM: all daily weather; precip_in_1d is dead last (perm ~0.000).

## KNOWN NEGATIVE RESULTS - do not naively re-propose these
- Lagged weather copies: HURT badly (loso_r2 0.116 -> 0.019)
- Rolling precip / water balance as implemented: worse (lofo_r2 0.013 vs 0.003)
- Broadcasting 2017 N-surplus forward in time: much worse (-0.166)
- Rolling (3D/7D) smoothed targets: worse
- Spike / anomaly z-score targets: failed cross-site (lofo_r2 ~ -0.0006)
- Antecedent moisture + rain x surplus interactions: REG a wash, CLF only +0.017 PR-AUC
- Riparian 0-2km bucket: CLF +0.039 PR-AUC but REG worse
- Advective travel-time routing IS ALREADY IMPLEMENTED (weather per distance bucket shifted by median flow distance / 2.1 m/s) and is part of the "lagged weather hurt" failure.
PATTERN: nearly every hydrologically-motivated TEMPORAL feature has failed. The only wins came from geometry and static geography. This strongly suggests the deficit is in BETWEEN-SITE static information, not in temporal dynamics.

## Data present on disk but UNUSED
- discharge/streamflow: only 22 of 85 sites (all USGS, 0.66-0.97 density, up to 18 years). ZERO of the 61 IWQIS sites.
- co-located water chemistry: specific conductance (65 sites), water temp (80), pH (64), dissolved oxygen (64), turbidity + phosphate (61)
- upstream_uid (28 sites) / downstream_uid (40 sites) river-network topology: completely unread
- draining_area (80/85), NHDPlus comid (stored per basin), basin containment graph (used only to build CV folds)

## Known data problems
- Nitrogen surplus (gTREND product) ENDS IN 2017 -> NaN for 68% of training rows
- 16.5% of grid cells lack crop/surplus data; an inner join silently UNDER-COUNTS crop area and N surplus for basins extending outside Iowa (worst for the largest multi-state basins)
- Tile drainage density: known to be the dominant hydrologic control in Iowa, NOT in the feature set, and NO data source has been identified yet


## Non-negotiable rules for this research

1. RECORD THE SPLIT PROTOCOL FOR EVERY PERFORMANCE NUMBER, AND DO NOT COMPARE NUMBERS ACROSS PROTOCOLS. Random-split results are valid evidence about method behavior and should be reported - researchers using them often have good reasons for their own question. But only SPATIALLY HELD-OUT numbers (leave-one-basin-out, leave-one-region-out, ungauged-basin protocol) are comparable to our LOFO 0.820, because a random split over autocorrelated site-days lets a model memorize a site's level and measures interpolation rather than transfer. When the protocol cannot be determined, say so rather than guessing.
2. REPORT EFFECT SIZES AND SAMPLE SIZES, NOT CONCLUSIONS. "GNNs improve water quality prediction" is worthless. "Recurrent GCN, 456 reaches, 42 monitored, held-out-node RMSE 1.83 vs 2.11 for LSTM" is actionable. Always give the number of catchments/basins/sites used.
3. EVERY DATASET RECOMMENDATION MUST BE OPERATIONAL: exact name, spatial resolution, temporal resolution, coverage years, whether it covers ALL of Iowa AND the multi-state portions of basins, exact URL, access mechanism (API/bulk/FTP), authentication requirement, and license.
4. ACTIVELY HUNT FOR NEGATIVE RESULTS. Seven feature-engineering ablations have already failed on this project. Papers reporting that a technique did NOT transfer are as valuable as successes and are systematically under-published - look in discussion/limitations sections and in benchmark comparison papers.
5. FLAG THE n=19-FAMILIES CONSTRAINT against every recommendation. If a method's evidence base comes from 300+ basins, say so explicitly and assess whether it can work at n=19.
6. ACQUISITION CONSTRAINT: recommend only free/public data, or data obtainable by a reasonable request (e.g. emailing IIHR or Iowa DNR). No paid datasets, no field campaigns, no new sensor deployment.
7. Prefer peer-reviewed literature and authoritative agency sources over blog posts. Give DOIs where they exist.
8. JUDGE EVERYTHING AGAINST THE DEPLOYMENT TARGET: an arbitrary ungauged map pin with no local history. State plainly when a method only works at gauged sites.


## Your assignment: synthesize the findings for angle "Prediction in Ungauged Basins: what regionalization transfers, and what is the ceiling"

### Research question
In the 25+ years of Prediction in Ungauged Basins (PUB) and catchment-similarity/regionalization literature, which regionalization strategy (spatial proximity, physical-attribute similarity, regression on catchment attributes, donor-catchment transfer, hierarchical/partial pooling) gives the largest skill gain when predicting a CONCENTRATION or EXCEEDANCE signal at an unmonitored site? And critically: what BETWEEN-BASIN skill (R2 of site means, or equivalent) do published studies actually attain when they have fewer than ~100 donor catchments?

### What a good answer contains
A ranked comparison of regionalization families with reported effect sizes. Explicit evidence on how skill SCALES WITH NUMBER OF DONOR CATCHMENTS (a curve or table, not an assertion). At least 2-3 papers doing WATER QUALITY PUB rather than streamflow PUB - and if none exist, say so plainly, because that absence is itself a finding. The standard evaluation protocol. A verdict on whether attribute-based similarity beats plain spatial proximity in flat, agriculturally homogeneous regions - note that lat/lon are already top-3 features for us, suggesting proximity may already be doing this work. Seeds: Bloschl et al. "Runoff Prediction in Ungauged Basins" (IAHS PUB Decade); Hrachowitz et al. 2013 "A decade of PUB"; Razavi & Coulibaly 2013 regionalization review; Oudin et al. catchment similarity.

### TIER 3 - UNVERIFIED claims
These were extracted from real sources but were NEVER adversarially verified - verification was cut to conserve budget. The characteristic failure mode in this corpus is CONFIDENT OVERREACH FROM THIN EVIDENCE, not fabrication: a claim's conclusion is often right while its stated warrant is wrong, its effect size misattributed, or its split protocol misdescribed.

STRICT RULES for tier 3, which you MUST follow:
- USE them for COVERAGE and LEADS: naming a dataset, a URL, an access route, a candidate attribute, or an angle worth pursuing.
- DO NOT use them as the warrant for any numeric performance figure, any effect size, or the core argument of any recommendation. Those must rest on verified (tier 1) claims.
- Any finding that rests on tier 3 MUST set confidence to "unverified" and say so in the claim text itself.
- If a tier 3 claim contradicts a verified claim, the verified claim wins; note the conflict.

Produce the structured finding set for this angle as JSON.

Merge semantic duplicates. Apply every correction supplied by the verifiers. Rank findings by relevance to the BETWEEN-SITE gap specifically. For each finding give feasibilityAtN19 and worksAtUngaugedPin honestly. Populate "datasets" for every concrete data source, with howToIncorporate written concretely enough to act on - name the feature that would be created and how it would be aggregated to a basin. Populate "uncovered" for any part of the question that produced nothing verifiable - absence of evidence must be reported as absence, never silently dropped. Your "verdict" must state plainly whether this angle is worth pursuing and why.

Output JSON with keys: angle, verdict, findings[] (each: claim, confidence, effectSize, splitProtocol, nBasins, sources[], feasibilityAtN19, worksAtUngaugedPin), datasets[] (each: name, url, resolution, years, access, license, coversMultiState, whyUseful, howToIncorporate, limitations), refuted[], uncovered[].

tier1_survived.claim: Pool, Vis & Seibert (2021) compared 19 regionalization approaches plus 4 benchmarks (23 methods total) for transferring HBV parameter sets to ungauged catchments, using 671 CAMELS catchments in the conterminous US under a leave-one-out cross-validation in which each catchment in turn is treated as ungauged and predicted from donor catchments. Each donor supplied its 10 calibrated parameter sets; predictions were the ensemble mean hydrograph over 30 (flexible region-of-influence) to 40-2,300 (classification-based) parameterizations, simulated 1 Oct 1989 - 30 Sep 1999. This leave-one-catchment-out design is the standard PUB evaluation protocol and is spatially held out at the catchment level, though donors may be spatially adjacent (no nesting/region blocking is applied, unlike our leave-one-basin-family-out).
tier1_survived.effectSize: 19 regionalization approaches + 4 benchmarks, leave-one-out over 671 catchments, HBV, 1989-1999 evaluation window
corrections:
The claim is accurate as stated and needs no factual correction. Five additions matter for how the parent uses it:

1. INTERNAL INCONSISTENCY IN THE PAPER, NOT THE CLAIM. The abstract and Section 2.3.1 say 19 regionalization approaches (19+4=23 total), but the Table 2 caption reads "Description of the 18 Regionalization and 4 Benchmark Approaches Tested in This Study" (=22). The claim follows the abstract and main text, which is the defensible reading. Cite as "19 (Table 2 caption says 18; the paper is internally inconsistent)."

2. NO TEMPORAL HOLDOUT - THE SPATIAL HOLDOUT IS REAL BUT THE UPPER BENCHMARK IS OPTIMISTIC. Donors were calibrated on Oct 1989-Sep 1999 and every approach was also evaluated on that same decade (2 preceding years as warm-up only). The receiver catchment's own data are never used to predict it, so the spatial holdout is genuine and the claim's protocol label is right. But the upper benchmark UB is a local calibration scored in-sample, so the relative-performance metric R* is measured against an optimistically biased ceiling. Do not read R* values as out-of-sample skill ratios.

3. EFFECTIVE n IS BELOW 671 FOR SOME APPROACHES. For Climate class, WB class, and Sign class, "Ungauged catchments that did not belong to any class were excluded from the evaluation." The 671 figure is exact for the dataset and for flexible-donor approaches, not uniformly for all 23 methods.

4. TRANSFERABILITY - THE BEST-PERFORMING APPROACHES ARE UNUSABLE AT OUR DEPLOYMENT TARGET. This is the most important caveat and the claim does not mention it. The winning categories all require target-site observations. The paper says of its category D/E methods that they "require either estimates of hydrological signatures or a small number of local point observations," and category D is premised on being able "to directly conduct a number of discharge measurements." Volume information was the single best similarity indicator (0.80). Our product is an arbitrary map pin with no nitrate history, no discharge gauge, and no guaranteed gauged upstream neighbor, so Vol, RMSE, Sign, Dist & Vol, Dist & Sign, Dist & RMSE, Attr & Sign and Qobs transfer are all off the table. The deployable subset is Dist (0.79), Attr (0.78), and fixed classifications (0.76), against a random-donor floor of 0.70. So the honest headroom for a no-local-data regionalization scheme in this study is roughly 0.06-0.09 RNP over random donor selection, not the 0.82 headline.

5. TRANSFERABILITY - THREE STRUCTURAL MISMATCHES WITH OUR SETTING.
   (a) n=19 CONSTRAINT BITES HARD. Every flexible approach selects the 3 most similar donors from a pool of 670. Lesson (b), "almost perfect donors exist for most catchments," is a property of a large diverse donor pool - with 670 candidates you can almost always find 3 close analogs. At 19 independent basin families, "3 nearest of 18" samples the similarity space far more coarsely and there is no basis to assume near-perfect donors exist. This paper's evidence base is ~35x our effective n and its central optimistic finding is the one most dependent on pool size. Flag it as likely infeasible at our scale.
   (b) CAMELS EXPLICITLY EXCLUDES OUR CATCHMENT TYPE. The 671 basins are selected for "minimal human influence" (Newman et al. 2015). Iowa row-crop, tile-drained, fertilized basins are precisely the heavily managed catchments screened out of CAMELS. The donor pool contains essentially no hydrologic analog to our target population, so the reported transferability of donor-selection rules is not demonstrated for tile-drained agricultural systems.
   (c) WRONG TARGET AND WRONG MODEL CLASS. This is streamflow hydrograph regionalization - transferring conceptual rainfall-runoff PARAMETERS of a bucket model - evaluated with KGE-family metrics. It contains no water-quality content whatsoever, and nothing about concentration, exceedance, or classification metrics such as AUC/PR-AUC. Our XGBoost is not a donor-transfer scheme; it already pools all sites globally. The paper's value here is conceptual (donor selection and similarity-based regionalization, plus the discipline of upper/lower/regionalization benchmarks and multi-criteria evaluation), not a method that can be lifted into our pipeline. Its most directly usable idea for us is lesson (c) plus the benchmarking framework: define an explicit lower benchmark (random/base-rate) and an upper benchmark (a site-calibrated model) and report performance relative to that spread - which is a reporting discipline, not a between-site accuracy gain.

The claim is accurate in every quoted number and in its protocol description; no refutation is warranted. Three additions are needed before it is used as support for anything.

(a) PROTOCOL, precise form: the split is spatially held out at the catchment level but has NO temporal holdout - donor parameters were calibrated on 1 Oct 1989 - 30 Sep 1999 and the regionalized predictions were evaluated on that same window. The claim's "spatial-holdout" label is correct but should be stated as "spatial holdout only, calibration and evaluation periods identical."

(b) INTERNAL INCONSISTENCY IN THE PAPER (not an error in the claim): the abstract and Section 2.3.1 body text say 19 regionalization approaches and "a total of 23 methods," but the Table 2 caption reads "Description of the 18 Regionalization and 4 Benchmark Approaches Tested in This Study" (=22). The claim follows the abstract/body, which is the defensible reading, but anyone quoting "19+4=23" should know Table 2 says 18+4.

(c) MATERIAL OMISSION FOR OUR DEPLOYMENT TARGET: a large share of the 19 approaches CANNOT be applied at an ungauged map pin. Categories D and E (Vol, RMSE, Sign, Attr & Sign, Dist & Vol, Dist & Sign, Dist & Attr & Sign, Dist & RMSE) are described by the authors as requiring "either estimates of hydrological signatures ... or a small number of local point observations" at the supposedly ungauged catchment, and Qobs transfer requires observed hydrographs from neighbors. The paper's headline winner - distance-plus-volume, median R_NP 0.82 - is in that group. The methods genuinely available with no local observations are the distance-only and attribute-only families at median R_NP 0.79 and 0.78, versus 0.70 for random donors. The usable no-local-data margin over random is therefore roughly 0.08-0.09 R_NP, not the 0.12 implied by the top-ranked method.

TRANSFERABILITY TO THIS PROJECT (flagging the n=19 constraint): the evidence base is 671 donor catchments, ~35x our 19 independent basin families. The mechanism transferred is a calibrated conceptual-model parameter vector, which has no analogue in a feature-based XGBoost classifier - so this paper does not supply a method we can implement, only a protocol design and a set of donor-selection heuristics. The flexible region-of-influence approaches select the 3 most similar donors from 670; at n=19 families a 3-donor region of influence draws from 18, so the donor pool is thin enough that the paper's central comparison (flexible RoI beating fixed classification) is untestable here. Target variable also differs fundamentally: daily streamflow evaluated with KGE variants, median catchment area 341 km2, versus our binary daily nitrate exceedance in tile-drained Iowa agricultural basins. Cite this paper for PUB protocol design and for the negative-ish result that attribute-based donor selection lands mid-rank (0.78) and barely beats spatial proximity (0.79), which is consistent with our own finding that static geography carries the between-site signal. Do not cite it as evidence that any regionalization method will deliver gains at n=19.

The claim is accurate as stated; only two refinements and a set of usage caveats are needed.

REFINEMENT 1 (internal inconsistency in the source, not in the claim): the paper's running text and abstract say 19 regionalization approaches and state "a total of 23 methods," but the caption of Table 2 reads "Description of the 18 Regionalization and 4 Benchmark Approaches Tested in This Study" (18+4=22). The claim reproduces the paper's own dominant wording (19+4=23); the discrepancy is the authors', not the claimant's. Cite it as "19 approaches (Table 2 caption says 18) plus 4 benchmarks."

REFINEMENT 2 (protocol, important for our rules): the holdout is SPATIAL ONLY. Donor parameter sets were calibrated on the same window they were evaluated on — "Calibration and evaluation were conducted during the simulation period from October 1, 1989 to September 30, 1999." There is no temporal holdout, and no nesting or region blocking, so this protocol is WEAKER than our leave-one-basin-family-out. Numbers from this study must not be treated as an upper bound comparable to LOFO transfer, and none of its metrics (R_NP/R_KG on daily hydrographs) are comparable to our AUC/PR-AUC on a binary exceedance target in any case.

USAGE CAVEATS FOR OUR PROJECT (the claim is true but should not be used to motivate donor-based regionalization here):

(a) The n=19-families constraint is fatal for the method family this paper evaluates, and the paper's own Figure 1 analysis quantifies why. With 670 candidate donors: "for a relative performance value of 0.7, half of the hypothetically ungauged catchments have at most 23 suitable donor catchments" — i.e. the median catchment has roughly 3.4% of the pool as usable donors. Scaled to our 18 available donor families, the expected number of suitable donors is well under one. The paper also reports that for the median catchment MOST donors are worse than random parameter sets ("For the other 60% of the donor catchments, one would be better off using random parameter sets"). Donor-transfer regionalization derives essentially all its power from a large, hydroclimatically diverse donor pool; at n=19 the pool is too small for the selection step to find anything.

(b) The two best-performing approach families are unavailable at our deployment target. The paper's own conclusion is that approaches combining spatial proximity with VOLUME information (streamflow-derived signatures) rank highest — and it concedes "volume information is per definition missing in ungauged catchments," recoverable only "from a small number of field measurements" or regionalized signatures. Our product pin has no discharge, and only 22 of 85 training sites have streamflow at all (zero of the 61 IWQIS sites), so we cannot even build the donor-side signature library statewide.

(c) Two of the four benchmarks are oracles, not deployable methods. UB requires calibrating on the target's own observations; Best requires knowing the target's observed hydrograph to rank donors by R_NP. The impressive "median 0.87, close to local calibration" number is an oracle ceiling, not an achievable ungauged result. The achievable numbers are the 0.76 (classification-based) to ~0.8x range against a 0.69–0.70 random-donor floor.

(d) Domain mismatch is large: HBV rainfall-runoff parameter transfer for daily streamflow in largely undisturbed CAMELS reference catchments, versus nitrate exceedance classification in tile-drained Iowa row-crop basins. CAMELS gauges are selected for minimal human disturbance, which excludes precisely the artificially drained, fertilized agricultural systems we model; tile drainage is not represented in HBV at all. The transferable insight is conceptual, not numerical: it corroborates our own finding that the hard part is the between-site absolute level, and that similarity must be defined on the right attributes — but it offers no evidence that donor-based transfer will work at n=19 with no volume information.

tier1_survived.claim: In Pool et al. (2021), the ranked medians across 671 US catchments (metric R_NP, a Nash-Sutcliffe-type relative efficiency; R_KG is the Kling-Gupta analogue) were: local calibration upper benchmark R_NP 0.89; best-3-available-donors oracle 0.87; spatial-distance + volume combinations 0.82 / R_KG 0.67; volume/signature similarity alone 0.80 / 0.66; spatial proximity alone 0.79 / 0.64; catchment attributes (physical similarity) alone 0.78 / 0.62; fixed classification-based donor pools 0.76 / 0.58; random donors 0.69-0.70 / 0.49. The entire spread from random donors to the best realizable method is therefore about 0.13 R_NP, and the spread between the three single-information families (volume 0.80, distance 0.79, attributes 0.78) is only 0.02 R_NP - i.e. choosing among proximity, attribute similarity, and signature similarity is nearly a wash relative to choosing any of them over random.
tier1_survived.effectSize: median R_NP: UB 0.89, best-donor oracle 0.87, Dist&Vol 0.82, Vol 0.80, Dist 0.79, Attr 0.78, classification 0.76, Random 0.69; total realizable gain over random ~0.13 R_NP
corrections:
The claim is accurate in every number, the source attribution, the protocol label, and n. Two corrections of framing, the first of which is decisive for our deployment target.

(1) THE THREE "SINGLE-INFORMATION FAMILIES" ARE NOT AN EQUAL-COST CHOICE SET — VOLUME REQUIRES THE TARGET'S OWN OBSERVATIONS. The claim implies picking among proximity, attributes, and volume/signature is a free choice that is "nearly a wash." It is a wash in score, but not in data requirements. Table 2 defines Vol verbatim as "The three catchments with the smallest volume error for the (hypothetically) ungauged catchment are used as donors" — i.e. the volume error is computed against the receiver's measured discharge. Section 2.3.1 category D states these methods assume "it is possible to estimate hydrological signatures for the ungauged catchment... or to directly conduct a number of discharge measurements," and category E (Dist & Vol) states outright: "These approaches also require either estimates of hydrological signatures or a small number of local point observations." So Vol (0.80) and the Dist&Vol category (0.82) are partial-oracle methods, and Best (0.87) is a full oracle (three best donors "defined by RNP," which needs the receiver's full observed hydrograph).

For OUR deployment target — an arbitrary map pin with zero local observations — the realizable menu is only: spatial proximity 0.79, catchment attributes 0.78, fixed classification 0.76, against random 0.69. The zero-observation spread over random is therefore ~0.10 R_NP, not 0.13, and the spread between the two usable single-information families (Dist 0.79 vs Attr 0.78) is 0.01, not 0.02. The claim's headline conclusion actually gets STRONGER for us: among methods we can actually deploy, proximity and attribute similarity are within 0.01 of each other and both are worth ~0.10 over random. The "0.82 best realizable" figure should not be quoted in our context without the local-observation caveat.

(2) TRANSFERABILITY TO SUSTAG IS WEAK ON FOUR AXES, AND THE n=19 CONSTRAINT BITES HARD AND ASYMMETRICALLY.
- Donor-pool size is the mechanism, and we do not have it. The paper's central Lesson (b) is that "almost perfect donors exist for most catchments" — that is a direct function of choosing the 3 best from a pool of 670. Our pool is ~18 other independent basin families. Both the oracle ceiling (0.87) and the realizable gain over random shrink monotonically with pool size, and the paper offers no evidence at small n. This is a 671-basin result and must be flagged as likely infeasible at n=19: with 18 candidate donors, the nearest neighbor in attribute space is often not near at all. The paper's own Random baseline (3 of 670) is also a much stronger baseline than 3-of-18 would be, so even the direction of the gap is not safely portable.
- Wrong physical system. CAMELS is explicitly screened for minimally-impacted, near-natural catchments. Iowa row-crop basins are artificially drained; the attribute vector Pool et al. use for similarity (area, aridity, precipitation seasonality, snowfall fraction, wetland fraction, clay fraction, forest fraction) contains nothing resembling tile-drainage density, the control our own notes flag as dominant.
- Wrong target. This is calibrated-parameter transfer for streamflow — a mass-conserving water-balance quantity — evaluated by NSE-type efficiency. It is not evidence about transferring the ABSOLUTE LEVEL of a nitrate exceedance rate, which is our actual between-site deficit (between_r2 0.21, between_rate_r2 0.24). Nothing in this paper speaks to concentration or exceedance regionalization.
- Wrong model class. The finding concerns donor selection for parameter transfer in a conceptual bucket model (HBV). It does not translate into a feature for a gradient-boosted classifier. The legitimate reading for us is narrow and methodological: it is evidence that ATTRIBUTE-SIMILARITY-BASED transfer is not meaningfully worse than SPATIAL-PROXIMITY-BASED transfer, which mildly discourages spending effort on elaborate similarity metrics and mildly supports the observation that our lat/lon features already capture much of what attribute similarity would. It is NOT evidence that improving static between-site descriptors (e.g. acquiring tile-drainage data) is futile — Pool et al. hold the attribute set fixed and vary only the donor-selection rule, so the study says nothing about the value of a BETTER attribute, only about the value of a better rule for using a fixed attribute set.

The claim is numerically exact — every median (UB 0.89, Best 0.87, Dist&Vol 0.82/RKG 0.67, Vol 0.80/0.66, Dist 0.79/0.64, Attr 0.78/0.62, classification 0.76/0.58, Random 0.69–0.70/0.49) is verbatim from Pool, Vis & Seibert (2021), WRR 57(10), doi:10.1029/2021WR030437, 671 CAMELS catchments, HBV, leave-one-out cross-validation. Four corrections of detail:

(1) METRIC. R_NP is the non-parametric variant of the KLING-GUPTA efficiency (Pool, Vis & Seibert 2018), not a "Nash-Sutcliffe-type" metric, and it is an ABSOLUTE efficiency. The paper's relative efficiency is a separate metric, R*_NP, defined as percent improvement over random donors bounded by local calibration. R_KG is the standard KGE; R_NP is the non-parametric analogue OF R_KG, reversing the claim's framing.

(2) "BEST REALIZABLE" IS WRONG FOR AN UNGAUGED PIN. Both Dist&Vol (0.82) and Vol (0.80) are defined using the TARGET CATCHMENT'S OWN OBSERVED DISCHARGE — Table 2: "the three catchments with the smallest volume error for the (hypothetically) ungauged catchment." Sign likewise uses the target's observed signatures. For a target with NO local observations — this project's deployment case — the best method in the study is Dist at 0.79, so the realizable spread over random is ~0.09–0.10 R_NP, not 0.13. The 0.13 figure is only achievable if you can measure flow at the "ungauged" site.

(3) THE "NEARLY A WASH" GLOSS IS A MEDIAN-ONLY STATEMENT AND THE PAPER EXPLICITLY WARNS AGAINST IT. §3.2.1: approaches "differ considerably in their poorest performance values leading to clear differences in the suitability of the approaches"; under random donors 44/671 catchments fell to R_NP between −0.2 and −11.6. Lesson 3 states the ranking "depends more on how the predicted hydrographs are evaluated than on how the donor catchments are calibrated" — under R_KG the same three families spread 0.04, double the R_NP spread. Per-catchment the best method varies widely (Dist&Vol 22%, Dist&Sign 12%, Vol/Sign 9%, marginal approaches 2–4% each).

(4) SAMPLE-SIZE / TRANSFER CAVEAT THAT MUST ACCOMPANY ANY USE OF THIS RESULT. Each target had 670 candidate donors; this project has 18. The paper attributes distance-based methods' advantage directly to high US gauge density (citing Lebecherel et al. 2016; Neri et al. 2020) and attributes classification-pool degradation to donor-pool heterogeneity — both mechanisms predict that donor-selection comparisons collapse at n=19 basin families. The study also concerns daily streamflow from a conceptual rainfall-runoff model in "minimal human influence" CAMELS catchments, not nitrate exceedance in tile-drained agricultural basins, and concerns transferring calibrated model parameters, not features for a gradient-boosted classifier. Finally, if this result is being used to argue that static catchment attributes are not worth pursuing, it argues the opposite: Attr alone gains +0.09 R_NP over random, roughly 70% of the entire no-local-data realizable gain.

The claim's numbers are exact — all eight medians, both metrics, n=671, and the spatial-holdout (leave-one-catchment-out) protocol are verbatim correct against the published paper, and the 0.13 and 0.02 arithmetic is right. Three corrections, one of them material.

(1) MATERIAL: "spatial-distance + volume combinations 0.82" is NOT "the best realizable method" for an ungauged site, and volume/signature similarity is not a third co-equal information family. Pool et al. define Vol as picking donors with "the smallest volume error for the (hypothetically) ungauged catchment," and state in the Plain Language Summary that "volume information is per definition missing in ungauged catchments." Vol (0.80), Sign, Dist&Vol (0.82), and Dist&RMSE all require observations at the target; Best (0.87) is a full oracle on the target's hydrograph. Only Dist (0.79) and Attr (0.78) are usable at an arbitrary pin with no local history. Correct restatement: at a truly ungauged site the realizable ceiling is 0.79 R_NP and the realizable gain over random donors is ~0.10 R_NP, not 0.13; the spread between the two genuinely available information families (proximity 0.79, attributes 0.78) is 0.01 R_NP, not 0.02. This makes the claim's core "nearly a wash" conclusion stronger, not weaker, but the claim as written would mislead anyone into thinking a 0.82-level method is available to this product.

(2) Metric gloss is inverted: R_KG is the Kling-Gupta efficiency (Gupta et al. 2009); R_NP is its non-parametric variant (Pool et al. 2018), using Spearman rank correlation and a normalized flow-duration-curve error. Neither is a Nash-Sutcliffe-type efficiency, and R_KG is not an "analogue" of R_NP — the derivation runs the other way.

(3) Random donors is reported as 0.69 in the benchmark section (Fig. 2) and 0.7 in the ranking section; the claim's "0.69-0.70" is a fair reconciliation but should be cited as two separate statements in the paper rather than a range the authors give.

Scope caveats to attach whenever this claim is used for SUSTAG: the evidence base is 671 near-natural CAMELS catchments doing HBV rainfall-runoff parameter transfer, not agricultural tile-drained basins doing water-quality exceedance classification; and the mechanism (select 3 most-similar donors from a pool of 670) does not survive reduction to 19 independent basin families, where 3 donors is ~17% of the available pool and the similarity region collapses toward the pool mean. Use this result as weak evidence that reshuffling static-geography feature encodings is low-yield — not as evidence about the size of the between-site headroom, which the paper's own 0.89-vs-0.69 UB-to-random gap and its "almost perfect donors exist for most catchments" lesson indicate is large.

tier3_unverified.claim: Kratzert et al. (2019, HESS 23:5089-5110, doi:10.5194/hess-23-5089-2019) did NOT test prediction in ungauged basins. The paper states explicitly: 'we never ask our model to predict in a basin where it did not see training data.' Training used calibration-period data (Oct 1999-Sep 2008) from all 531 CAMELS basins and evaluation used validation-period data (Oct 1989-Sep 1999) from the SAME 531 basins. Therefore every NSE figure in this paper is a TEMPORAL holdout on gauged basins and is NOT comparable to a leave-one-basin-out / LOFO number. This paper is routinely mis-cited as PUB evidence; the actual PUB companion is Kratzert et al. 2019 WRR (doi:10.1029/2019WR026065), which used k-fold spatial holdout.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: n/a - protocol claim
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 531 (447 for benchmark-model comparison)

tier3_unverified.claim: With a temporal (not spatial) holdout on 531 CAMELS basins, a single regional EA-LSTM reached mean NSE 0.67 +/- 0.006 / median NSE 0.71; the 8-member ensemble reached mean NSE 0.71 / median NSE 0.74. A standard LSTM fed the same static attributes was statistically indistinguishable (single: mean 0.66 / median 0.70; ensemble: mean 0.70 / median 0.73). The architectural innovation (entity-aware static input gate) bought essentially NOTHING in accuracy - its value was claimed to be interpretability of the learned catchment embedding, not skill.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: EA-LSTM vs LSTM+static: +0.01 mean NSE, +0.01 median NSE (within noise)

tier3_unverified.claim: On the same 531-basin temporal holdout, a single regionally-trained LSTM/EA-LSTM outperformed hydrological models CALIBRATED INDIVIDUALLY PER BASIN (on the 447 commonly-modeled subset): EA-LSTM ensemble mean NSE 0.71 vs basin-calibrated HBV-ensemble 0.61, mHM 0.59, SAC-SMA 0.52, VIC 0.52. Regionally-calibrated conceptual models were far worse: mHM 0.44, VIC 0.17. Interpretation for our project: the gap between regional calibration (0.17-0.44) and per-basin calibration (0.52-0.61) quantifies the classic 'between-site level' penalty, and ML closed it ONLY by having 531 gauged donors to learn the attribute->behavior mapping from.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: regional ML 0.71 mean NSE vs regionally-calibrated VIC 0.17 / mHM 0.44; vs basin-calibrated best (HBV) 0.61

tier3_unverified.claim: Static catchment attributes were the load-bearing component, not the meteorological time series. Removing the 27 static CAMELS attributes and training on meteorology alone collapsed performance: the paper reports the with-attributes model improved mean NSE by approximately 0.44 over the no-attributes model (no-static mean NSE reported around 0.39 under one loss configuration - exact per-cell table values should be re-verified against Table 3 of the published PDF, as our extraction of the no-static row was second-hand). Directional claim is robust and directly supports this project's diagnosis that the deficit is BETWEEN-SITE static information, not temporal dynamics.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: ~+0.44 mean NSE from adding 27 static attributes; exact no-static row flagged as needing verification

tier3_unverified.claim: An attribute-corruption robustness test showed graceful, non-brittle degradation: adding Gaussian noise to the standardized static catchment attributes moved median NSE from 0.71 (no noise) to ~0.71 at sigma=0.1, ~0.65 at sigma=0.25, ~0.55 at sigma=0.5, and 0.48 at sigma=1.0. The authors argue this smoothness shows the network learned a generalizable attribute->behavior mapping rather than memorizing basin identity. Falsifiable implication for us: if a model's skill is genuinely attribute-driven rather than lat/lon-memorization, jittering the static features should degrade skill smoothly and monotonically; a cliff would indicate identity memorization. This is a cheap ablation we can replicate at n=19 families.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: median NSE 0.71 -> 0.48 across sigma 0 -> 1.0 standardized-attribute noise

tier3_unverified.claim: The paper contains NO experiment on how skill scales with the number of training/donor basins - performance is never reported as a function of training-set size, and no learning curve over basin count is presented. It also contains NO water-quality content whatsoever; the entire study is daily streamflow. Consequently this paper provides ZERO direct evidence that a 531-basin-derived regionalization result transfers to an n=19-independent-family, concentration/exceedance problem. Its clustering analysis (k-means on the 256-dim embedding produced more distinct catchment clusters than k-means on the raw 27 attributes) is qualitative and reported without a held-out predictive metric.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: none reported - absence of scaling curve and absence of water-quality evidence is the finding

tier3_unverified.claim: Willard et al. (2024) trained on 782 CONUS stream-temperature sites (>=5 years of data, ~3.82M observations) and evaluated on 580 DIFFERENT held-out sites treated as 'unmonitored' — a genuinely spatial ungauged-basin protocol (single train/test site split, not k-fold, no site appears in both). Total pool 1,362 sites, 4,378,876 observations. This is the standard PUB evaluation protocol and is the protocol class comparable to our LOFO numbers.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: n/a — protocol description

The pooled model won in 14/17 regions and 14/15 attribute clusters. Directly falsifies the 'group basins by similarity then fit locally' regionalization family: partitioning the donor pool cost ~0.55-0.59degC RMSE (~40% worse).

The authors state adding location information 'did not meaningfully improve performance.' This is direct evidence that physical-attribute similarity beats plain spatial proximity as a regionalization signal, and that a model relying on lat/lon as a top feature is leaving between-site skill on the table.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: meteo 1.77 -> +latlon/elev 1.72 (delta 0.05) -> +GAGES-II 1.47 (delta 0.25) degC median RMSE

Requiring discharge also shrank the usable training pool from 1,346 to 1,048 sites (~4.65M obs). Relevant to our 22/85-site discharge coverage: the evidence says the coverage sacrifice is not worth it relative to investing in static basin attributes.

tier3_unverified.claim: The paper provides a partial data-volume-vs-feature-richness tradeoff rather than a clean site-count scaling curve: because meteorology+location inputs are universally available, that configuration could be trained on 2,999 candidate sites (~6.13M observations spanning 1,346 training sites) versus 782 sites (~3.82M obs) for the attribute-rich model, and requiring GAGES-II attributes cut the pool to 833 sites (~4.13M obs). Extended training data produced only 'similar or modest improvements' — i.e. roughly doubling the donor-site count did NOT close the gap created by missing static attributes. NEGATIVE FINDING for our project: no explicit ablation reducing donor count below ~780 basins exists in this paper, so it gives NO evidence about behavior at n=19 independent basin families; all its conclusions rest on 780-1,350 donors.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: ~1.6x more sites / 1.6x more observations yielded only 'similar or modest' RMSE improvement; feature richness dominated donor count
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 782 vs 1346 vs 1048 vs 833 training sites depending on required inputs; 580 held-out test

tier3_unverified.claim: This paper addresses ONLY stream temperature — no nitrate, nutrient, or any other water-quality constituent is modeled ('we have built several models to predict daily stream temperatures... as a case study'). Its stated failure mode is also physically specific: models are accurate where air temperature is the dominant control and degrade at sites 'impacted by groundwater and dams', with RMSE >2degC in the mountainous West. Stream temperature is a far more air-temperature-forced, lower-between-site-variance signal than nitrate concentration, so its 1.43degC unmonitored-site skill should NOT be read as an achievable ceiling for concentration/exceedance PUB; the absence of water-quality PUB evidence in this flagship continental-scale PUB benchmark is itself a finding.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: n/a — scope/negative-coverage claim
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 1362 (stream temperature only; 0 water-quality-constituent sites)

tier3_unverified.claim: Pool et al. (2021) found that spatial proximity outperformed physical-attribute similarity (median R_NP 0.79 vs 0.78; R_KG 0.64 vs 0.62) across 671 US catchments, consistent with Merz & Bloschl (2004), Oudin et al. (2008), Swain & Patra (2017) and Zhang & Chiew (2009), and attributed this explicitly to 'the relatively high gauging station density in many humid regions of the United States' and to 'the lack of catchment attributes representing a wide range of catchment responses over large scales'. They further cite Jehn et al. (2020) that non-climatic catchment attributes 'can vary considerably within hydrologically similar regions in the United States and can often not sufficiently explain hydrological behavior'. This supports the interpretation that raw lat/lon proximity already captures most of what attribute-similarity regionalization would add, especially in a dense-network, hydroclimatically homogeneous region.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Dist beats Attr by +0.01 median R_NP and +0.02 median R_KG

tier3_unverified.claim: Pool et al. (2021) report a NEGATIVE result directly relevant to attribute-based site ranking: when the three catchments most similar to the target in geographic, signature, or attribute space were selected as donors, 'the ranks of these most similar donors in the "performance space" are typically clearly worse than the ranks of the three best donors in the "characteristics space"'. Catchment similarity to the true best donors was highest for hydrological signatures, then spatial distance, and SMALLEST for physical attributes. In other words, similarity in measured catchment attributes is a poor proxy for transferability of behavior - the gap between the oracle donor (median R_NP 0.87) and any attribute-selected donor set (0.78) is a similarity-metric failure, not a modeling failure. The only similarity metrics that came close were combinations of Sign or Attr WITH Dist.

(2021) the methods that added VOLUME information - i.e. an estimate of the target's own mean streamflow level or signatures, obtainable from as few as 12 point observations (Pool et al. 2019; Rojas-Serna et al. 2016; Viviroli & Seibert 2015) - were the top-ranked family (Dist & Vol, median R_NP 0.82 / R_KG 0.67), and 'volume seemed to be the best similarity indicator'. The paper is explicit that this information 'is per definition missing in ungauged catchments' and must come from field measurements or from separately regionalized signature estimates. This is a CRITICAL CAVEAT for the map-pin deployment target: the top-performing regionalization family in the largest comparative PUB study requires a handful of observations AT the target site, which the shipped product does not have. It does, however, quantify what a small number of grab samples at a candidate pin would be worth: roughly +0.03 to +0.04 median R_NP over pure proximity.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Dist&Vol 0.82 vs Dist alone 0.79 median R_NP (+0.03); Vol-based selection used 12 targeted observations at the 'ungauged' site

tier3_unverified.claim: NEGATIVE / ABSENCE FINDING: Pool et al. (2021) contains NO water-quality, nitrate, or concentration prediction whatsoever - the words 'water quality', 'nitrate' and 'concentration' do not appear; all 671 catchments and all 19 approaches concern daily STREAMFLOW only. It also contains NO donor-pool-size or gauging-density experiment: skill-versus-number-of-donors is never varied (the donor pool is fixed at 670 for every catchment), and density effects are only asserted by citation to Lebecherel et al. (2016), Neri et al. (2020, doi:10.5194/hess-24-5149-2020, 209 Austrian catchments, nested catchments and gauging station density) and Parajka et al. (2015, top-kriging station density). The one cross-study anchor given is Neri et al. (2020): median R_KG 0.6-0.75 for 209 Austrian catchments regionalized by attribute similarity or spatial proximity, versus global-scale regression/classification regionalizations reaching only median monthly R_KG 0.32 (Arheimer et al. 2020) and 0.45 (Beck et al. 2016). Therefore this paper CANNOT be cited as evidence about performance at n=19 donor families, and its 671-catchment evidence base must be flagged as ~35x larger than our independent-unit count.

This is a water-quality (not streamflow) PUB result and reproduces the 'good timer, mediocre site-ranker' failure mode at continental scale with a deep-learning architecture.

(2025), making this one of the few published head-to-head measurements of the transfer penalty for daily nitrate CONCENTRATION prediction; the ungauged-basin number is the only one comparable to a leave-one-basin-out protocol.

The surplus-to-export relationship is therefore strongly wetness-conditional, suggesting an annual or seasonal basin wetness state variable (not a same-day or short-rolling precip term, both of which already failed here) is the mechanistically indicated interaction.

This is evidence that the between-site ceiling for nitrate is low as a property of the problem, and that adding donor catchments alone is not sufficient to close it.
