tier3_unverified.claim: Oudin et al. (2008) compared three regionalization families for transferring lumped rainfall-runoff model parameters to ungauged catchments across 913 French catchments using two models (TOPMO and GR4J), and found a stable rank order: spatial proximity best, physical similarity intermediate, regression on catchment attributes worst. Parajka et al. (2013), which tabulates this study in its PUB meta-analysis (Table 1), records Oudin's ungauged-mode Nash-Sutcliffe efficiencies as 0.69, 0.71, 0.55, 0.71, 0.74, 0.68 for the model-averaging / proximity / regression combinations across the two models — i.e. proximity around NSE 0.71-0.74 versus regression around NSE 0.55-0.68. FALSIFIABLE: if the Wiley full text shows similarity outranking proximity, or shows regression within 0.02 NSE of proximity, this claim is wrong. CAVEAT: the mapping of the six numbers to specific (method, model) pairs is inferred from Parajka's method-code ordering 'MA, P, R' and should be verified against the original Tables.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Proximity NSE ~0.71-0.74 vs regression NSE ~0.55-0.68 across two models; gap of roughly 0.03-0.16 NSE depending on model. Consistent sign across both model structures.
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout — each gauged catchment treated in turn as ungauged (leave-one-out / pseudo-ungauged), donors drawn from the remaining catchments; Parajka et al. 2013 explicitly describe the cross-validation for this class of study as 'a leave-one-out strategy, where each gauged catchment was in turn considered as ungauged'
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 913 French catchments

tier3_unverified.claim: MOST DIRECTLY RELEVANT NEGATIVE RESULT FOR THIS PROJECT: Oudin et al. (2008) report verbatim in their abstract that 'The regression approach is the least satisfactory, with results very close to those obtained using one median parameter set for the whole country.' That is, regressing model behaviour on catchment physical attributes over 913 catchments recovered essentially NO between-catchment information beyond a single global constant. This is the exact functional analogue of our between-site problem: learning a site's absolute level from static basin attributes. With n=913 donor catchments — 48x our 19 independent basin families — attribute regression still failed to beat a constant. This is strong prior evidence that adding more static basin attributes (tile drainage, soils, additional land-use aggregates) to predict the ABSOLUTE LEVEL at an unseen Iowa basin will underperform expectations, and it argues that our lat/lon features being top-3 is the spatial-proximity mechanism already doing the work that attribute regression is failing to do.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Attribute regression ≈ single median global parameter set (difference described as 'very close'; no separation reported). Effectively zero between-catchment skill gain from attribute regression at n=913.
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 913 French catchments

tier3_unverified.claim: THE DONOR-DENSITY SCALING RESULT — the single most decision-relevant number found. Oudin et al. (2008) degraded the French gauging network to test how the proximity-vs-similarity ranking depends on donor density. Parajka et al. (2013, p. 1788) report: 'Oudin et al. (2008), for example, reported that spatial proximity slightly outperformed the similarity method in regions with a dense stream gauge network. They reported that the predictive performance of these two approaches becomes similar when the density of stream gauges decreases to less than 60 gauges per 100 000 km2.' DERIVED FOR IOWA (145,746 km2): our 85 sensor sites = 58 sites per 100,000 km2, and our 19 INDEPENDENT BASIN FAMILIES = 13 per 100,000 km2. Both are at or far below Oudin's 60/100,000 km2 threshold. FALSIFIABLE PREDICTION: at our donor density, spatial proximity should have NO reliable advantage over attribute similarity — the two should be statistically indistinguishable — and neither should be expected to reach the skill Oudin obtained at full French density. This directly predicts that swapping our lat/lon proximity signal for an attribute-similarity donor scheme will be a wash, not a win.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Proximity advantage over similarity shrinks to zero below ~60 gauges/100,000 km2. Iowa equivalents: 58 per 100,000 km2 at 85 sites; 13 per 100,000 km2 at 19 independent families.
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout (pseudo-ungauged leave-one-out) under progressively thinned donor networks
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 913 French catchments (Oudin), progressively thinned to lower densities; threshold stated at <60 gauges per 100,000 km2

tier3_unverified.claim: THE PUB CEILING, STATED BY THE AUTHORS: Oudin et al. (2008) abstract, verbatim: 'However, the results obtained with these three methods lag far behind those obtained by full model calibration... there is still considerable room for progress in the field of ungaged catchment modeling.' The best regionalization (proximity, NSE ~0.71-0.74) is substantially below what the same models achieve when calibrated on the target catchment's own observations. The authors also report that 'some improvement could be made by combining spatial proximity and physical similarity' — the ONLY positive lever they identify, and it is described as an improvement, not a fix. IMPLICATION FOR US: the gap we observe between within_r2 0.42 (temporal, site-informed) and between_r2 0.21 (transfer to unseen basin) is the canonical, expected, 25-year-unsolved PUB signature, not a defect specific to our feature set. Our project's 'good timer, mediocre site-ranker' diagnosis is the field's standard result restated.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: All three regionalization families 'lag far behind' full calibration (magnitude not quotable from abstract alone — the paywalled Tables would be needed). Combining proximity + similarity gives an unquantified improvement.
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout (pseudo-ungauged) compared against same-site full calibration — the two protocols are explicitly contrasted, which is the correct comparison to make and is exactly our within vs between decomposition
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 913 French catchments

tier3_unverified.claim: HOW SKILL SCALES WITH NUMBER OF DONOR CATCHMENTS — an actual curve, from Parajka et al. (2013) Figs. 4 and 5, Level 1 meta-analysis of 34 studies / 75 results / 3874 catchments. Findings, verbatim and paraphrased: (a) 'the 21 studies with less than 20 catchments have the largest scatter in the performance because of the smallest sample size'; (b) 'As the number of catchments increases the performance tends to decrease'; (c) 'For 12 studies with more than 250 catchments the performance however tends to increase.' The authors attribute the small-n advantage to selection bias, not method quality: 'in some of the studies with few catchments, these catchments were hand picked in terms of suitability for regionalisation and this happens less frequently in the studies with more catchments.' CRITICALLY for us: 'The maximum performance exceeds 0.8 for the similarity, regression and model averaging methods, but this performance is documented only for the small datasets. Interestingly, the performance of similarity-based regionalisation is clearly lower for assessments with large datasets.' Result counts by method: 33 spatial proximity, 9 similarity, 12 model averaging, 17 parameter regression, 4 regional calibration. FALSIFIABLE IMPLICATION AT OUR n=19: we sit in the highest-variance, most selection-biased stratum of the entire PUB literature. Any single-number regionalization gain we measure on 19 families carries scatter comparable to the full 0.3-0.9 NSE spread of that stratum, so a reported improvement of less than roughly 0.05 in our transfer metrics is not distinguishable from donor-set luck. This is an argument for repeated/nested CV over families and for reporting confidence intervals, NOT for abandoning regionalization.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Strata used: <20, 20-200, >200 catchments. Median NSE band across strata roughly 0.5-0.75 with the <20 stratum spanning ~0.3-0.9. Max NSE >0.8 for similarity/regression/model-averaging occurs ONLY in small datasets. Level 2 ranking over 1832 catchments: highest = similarity and spatial proximity (tied at top); lowest = model averaging. In humid catchments specifically: spatial proximity and similarity highest, model average lowest.
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout throughout — Level 2 performance 'estimated by a leave-one-out strategy, where each gauged catchment was in turn considered as ungauged and estimated runoff was compared with the observed runoff hydrographs'; Level 1 aggregates study-reported ungauged-mode results
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 34 studies, 75 results, 3874 catchments (Level 1); 9 studies, 1832 catchments (Level 2, of which 1479 humid and 353 arid)

tier3_unverified.claim: THE ABSENCE FINDING ON WATER-QUALITY PUB — reported plainly because the absence is itself the result. The IAHS PUB Decade's own flagship comparative assessment (Parajka et al. 2013, Part 1, with companion Parts by Salinas et al. 2013 and Viglione et al. 2013) surveys 34 studies and 3874 catchments and is ENTIRELY streamflow. A full-text search of the paper for 'water quality', 'nitrate', 'nutrient', and 'concentration' returns exactly ONE hit, and it is motivational rather than a study: environmental-change interest in 'the runoff hydrographs and water quality for which accurate runoff predictions are needed'. Not a single one of the 34 assessed studies predicts a concentration or an exceedance signal. Likewise Oudin et al. (2008), the largest-n regionalization comparison in the literature at 913 catchments, regionalizes rainfall-runoff MODEL PARAMETERS, not a water-quality state. CONSEQUENCE: there is no published water-quality PUB benchmark against which our LOFO AUC 0.820 / PR-AUC 0.634 can be compared, and every effect size quoted in this source transfers to us only by ANALOGY — streamflow regionalization skill is not evidence about nitrate concentration regionalization skill. Any claim that a regionalization technique 'works for water quality' on the strength of this literature is unsupported.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: 0 of 34 PUB studies / 0 of 3874 catchments address a concentration or exceedance target. 1 of 1 textual mentions of 'water quality' is motivational.
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: not-applicable — this is a claim about the absence of studies, not a performance number
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 3874 catchments across 34 studies, of which zero are water-quality studies

tier3_unverified.claim: Gorski et al. (2024) built deep-learning (LSTM-family) hindcasts of 7-day backward-looking average stream nitrate concentration at 46 predominantly agricultural sites in the midwestern and eastern US. SINGLE-SITE models -- trained AND tested at the same location, i.e. using that site's own nitrate history -- achieved a median Kling-Gupta Efficiency of 0.66. This is the paper's headline skill number and it is an INTERPOLATION result, not a transfer result: it is not comparable to our LOFO 0.820 AUC / R2 0.328, and it describes a setting our deployment target (arbitrary ungauged map pin, no local nitrate history) categorically does not have. VERIFIED FROM ABSTRACT ONLY -- Wiley full text returned HTTP 402/403 on all routes.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: median KGE = 0.66 across 46 sites, single-site models
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: temporal-holdout (within-site: 'trained and tested at a single location'; exact partition not verifiable from abstract)

tier3_unverified.claim: NEGATIVE RESULT ON GLOBAL POOLING FOR WATER QUALITY: in Gorski et al. (2024), 'developing a single model for all sites reduced performance at several locations with distinct characteristics, suggesting that there is a threshold of dissimilarity beyond which more data does not improve the model' (n=46 sites). This directly contradicts the streamflow-PUB/CAMELS finding that one large multi-basin model beats per-basin models. Falsifiable prediction for our project: naively pooling all 85 Iowa sites into one global model will degrade skill at the most hydrologically distinct basin families rather than improve them, and any gain must come from similarity-based grouping, not from adding rows. Per-site or per-group effect sizes are in the paywalled full text; only the directional claim is verified.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: direction only -- 'reduced performance at several locations'; magnitude not verifiable from abstract
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: unknown (comparison of all-site pooled vs single-site models; pooled model's spatial holdout status not determinable from abstract)

tier3_unverified.claim: ATTRIBUTE-SIMILARITY GROUPING BEAT BOTH EXTREMES: Gorski et al. (2024) report that 'accuracy at poorly performing sites could be improved by grouping sites with similar characteristics' (n=46). This ranks the regionalization families as: partial pooling by attribute similarity > single-site models (at weak sites) > full pooling across all sites (at distinct sites). This is the one piece of positive regionalization evidence in the paper and it is the family most compatible with our n=19-independent-basin-families constraint, since it requires only that families be clusterable, not that hundreds of donors exist. Number of groups used, grouping variables, and the KGE delta from grouping are in the paywalled full text and could NOT be verified.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: direction only -- improvement confined to 'poorly performing sites'; magnitude not verifiable from abstract
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: unknown (grouped-model evaluation protocol not determinable from abstract)

tier3_unverified.claim: EXPLICIT STATEMENT THAT THE STREAMFLOW-PUB TRANSFER RESULT DOES NOT CARRY OVER TO WATER QUALITY: Gorski et al. (2024) state 'While many deep learning studies have shown that national or even global models can outperform local models, it is not clear that this is true for water quality constituents.' This is an authoritative (USGS-coauthored, WRR) warning that the CAMELS-era evidence base (531-671 basins, streamflow) should NOT be assumed to transfer to nitrate. Consequence for our project: any recommendation whose evidence is streamflow regionalization at 300+ basins must be flagged as unvalidated for concentration/exceedance targets, independent of the separate n=19 sample-size objection.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: not-applicable
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: not-applicable (statement about the literature, not a measured result)

tier3_unverified.claim: DISCHARGE IS THE DOMINANT PREDICTOR, AND IT IS UNAVAILABLE AT OUR DEPLOYMENT TARGET: Gorski et al. (2024) report that 'across all sites, discharge and watershed soil and physiographic attributes showed a strong influence on model performance', with daily observed discharge used as a model INPUT at all 46 sites. Every skill number in this paper therefore presupposes a co-located streamflow gauge. Our shipped product has no discharge at an arbitrary map pin, and on-disk discharge exists at only 22 of 85 sites (zero of 61 IWQIS sites), so this paper's performance is not attainable by our architecture. The actionable residual is the SECOND-ranked driver group -- watershed soil and physiographic attributes -- which is static, map-derivable everywhere in Iowa, and is precisely the between-site information our model currently lacks (between_r2 0.21 vs within_r2 0.42).
tier3_unverified.effectSize: qualitative ranking only -- discharge + soil/physiographic attributes 'strong influence'; per-feature importances in paywalled full text

tier3_unverified.claim: THIS PAPER APPEARS TO CONTAIN NO UNGAUGED-BASIN (SPATIALLY HELD-OUT / LEAVE-SITE-OUT) EVALUATION. The abstract enumerates the model families tested -- single-site, similarity-grouped, all-site -- and describes them as ways to 'pool data across sites to develop accurate models and make the most effective use of available data', with no mention of predicting at a site withheld from training. Title framing ('at Intensively Monitored Sites') reinforces that the scope is data-rich monitored locations. If correct, this paper provides NO evidence about our actual problem and its KGE 0.66 must never be cited as a PUB benchmark. FALSIFIABLE AND UNRESOLVED: this must be checked against the full text (Section on model experiments / holdout design), which returned HTTP 402/403 on every access route tried (Wiley landing page, pdfdirect, DOAJ record, USGS Pubs Warehouse); Unpaywall lists no repository copy despite gold CC-BY status, and no ESSOAr/EarthArXiv/Authorea preprint exists.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: not-applicable
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: unknown -- no spatial holdout evident in abstract; requires full-text verification

tier3_unverified.claim: In a leave-one-catchment-out pseudo-ungauged experiment over 148 catchments in northeast North America (HYSETS, 1979-2018, drainage area >500 km2, >=30 years of record each), a single LSTM trained across all other catchments achieved median NSE 0.78 at held-out ungauged catchments, versus median NSE 0.58-0.63 for 18 combinations of three conceptual hydrological models (GR4JCN, HMETS, HSAMI) crossed with six regionalization schemes. The LSTM beat every one of the 18 model-regionalization combinations in at least 93% of catchments. This is a streamflow result, not a concentration or exceedance result.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: median NSE 0.78 (LSTM) vs 0.58-0.63 (18 HM-regionalization combos); LSTM superior in >=93% of basins

tier3_unverified.claim: An oracle-style upper bound on classical regionalization was computed: BEST-HM, which selects for each catchment the best-performing of all hydrological-model/regionalization combinations after the fact (information unavailable at a truly ungauged site), reached median NSE 0.66 - still below the LSTM's 0.78. This implies that no choice among the classical regionalization families (spatial proximity, physical similarity, multi-donor averaging, inverse distance weighting, donor filtering) closes the gap to a cross-catchment learned model, even with hindsight donor selection.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: BEST-HM oracle median NSE 0.66 vs LSTM 0.78 (+0.12 NSE)

tier3_unverified.claim: The LSTM applied in fully ungauged mode outperformed hydrological models that had been CALIBRATED ON THE TARGET CATCHMENT'S OWN OBSERVED FLOW in 73-78% of catchments (75% vs GR4JCN, 78% vs HMETS, 73% vs HSAMI). That is, cross-catchment learning with static attributes beat local calibration with local data for roughly three-quarters of sites - direct evidence that between-site information can be carried by attributes rather than by local history.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: LSTM >= locally-calibrated HM in 75% / 78% / 73% of basins
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout (LSTM) compared against locally-calibrated in-sample hydrological models

tier3_unverified.claim: NEGATIVE RESULT contradicting prior regionalization guidance: filtering out poorly-calibrated donor catchments (removing donors with calibration NSE < 0.7) did NOT increase regionalization skill. The authors state explicitly 'Removing poorly calibrated catchments did not increase overall regionalization skill, contrary to Oudin et al. (2008).' Similarly, regularization of the LSTM 'failed to improve results' in this study. The paper also reports that the choice of hydrological model mattered only marginally compared to the choice of regionalization method.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: donor-quality filtering: no measurable gain; median NSE across all 18 HM configs stayed within the narrow 0.58-0.63 band

tier3_unverified.claim: The paper provides NO scaling curve or sensitivity experiment on the number of donor/training catchments - a direct gap against the question of what skill is attainable with few donors. Every LSTM run used ~118 training catchments (80% of the 147 non-held-out basins) with 29 held for validation, and multi-donor hydrological regionalization used a fixed N=5 donors. The only quantitative data-volume guidance offered is temporal, citing Kratzert et al. (2018) that '15 years is a lower bound for the training' per catchment, and the authors required >=30 years of record per catchment. Therefore this paper CANNOT be used to argue the LSTM/cross-catchment advantage survives at n=19 independent basin families; its evidence base is ~118 training catchments with >=30 years each.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: no donor-count scaling experiment reported
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 148 total; ~118 training per fold; 5 donors for HM regionalization

tier3_unverified.claim: The regionalization signal was carried by 25 static basin-averaged descriptors supplied as LSTM inputs alongside meteorological forcings: mean elevation, mean slope, mean aspect, latitude, longitude, land-cover fractions (forest, shrub, grass, crop, urban, barren, water, snow/ice, wetland; from NALCMS 2010), mean annual precipitation, temperature, snowfall and rain, and an aridity index (precipitation over estimated PET); elevation from EarthENV 90 m DEM. The authors attribute the LSTM's edge to it being able to 'automatically parse and adjust the weights of catchment descriptors' rather than relying on a hand-specified donor-similarity metric. A stated architectural constraint is that 'the size of the inputs must remain the same throughout the training and regionalization process for all catchments' - i.e. no attribute may be missing for any basin, which is a hard blocker for attributes with partial coverage.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: 25 static descriptors; lat/lon included among them alongside physical attributes

tier3_unverified.claim: SCOPE LIMITATION relevant to the water-quality PUB question: this paper addresses streamflow only. It contains no water-quality, concentration, or exceedance-threshold prediction, and reports no separate numerical breakdown of spatial proximity (SP) versus physical similarity (PS) median NSE - Figure 4 shows box plots for both but the text makes no explicit claim that either family beats the other, stating only that 'the selection of the regionalization method plays a more significant role' than the choice of hydrological model. So this source does not settle whether attribute similarity beats plain spatial proximity in homogeneous terrain.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: SP vs PS difference not quantified in text; no water-quality results present

tier3_unverified.claim: The survey's own headline gap-finding, stated verbatim in the abstract: "most prior efforts have been focused on deep learning frameworks built on MANY SITES for predictions at daily time scales in the United States, but that comparisons between different classes of machine learning methods are few and inadequate." FALSIFIABLE IMPLICATION FOR US: the published PUB evidence base is built on large-n site pools (CAMELS 531, CONUS stream-temperature networks, 305 lakes); the survey identifies NO body of work establishing skill at n<100 donor units, and identifies NO head-to-head ranked comparison of regionalization families. Our n=19 independent basin families sits outside the regime this literature evidences. The survey also does NOT report any curve or table of skill vs number of donor catchments — we searched the full text specifically for this and it is absent, which is itself the finding: the scaling relationship the research question asks for is not established in the field's own 2025 survey.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: No quantitative skill-vs-n-donors curve exists in the survey; comparisons between ML method classes described by the authors as "few and inadequate"
tier3_unverified.nBasins: not-applicable — survey-level claim about the literature

tier3_unverified.claim: WATER QUALITY PUB IS NEARLY ABSENT AS A QUANTITATIVE LITERATURE. Despite the abstract promising review of "streamflow, water quality, and other water resources prediction," the survey's concrete unmonitored-site results are overwhelmingly streamflow, stream temperature and lake temperature. The only broad-scale water-quality-at-unmonitored-sites application named is "dissolved oxygen in streams," cited WITHOUT any performance metric, without a site count, and without a stated split protocol. No nitrate/nitrogen concentration PUB study with numbers appears. DIRECT ANSWER TO OUR RESEARCH QUESTION: the requested "2-3 papers doing water quality PUB rather than streamflow PUB" do not exist in quantified form in the field's most recent survey. Our LOFO CLF AUC 0.820 / PR-AUC 0.634 for nitrate exceedance therefore has NO published water-quality-PUB benchmark to be compared against, and any transfer of streamflow-PUB expectations (e.g. "LSTM matches calibrated models in ungauged basins") to a concentration/exceedance target is unevidenced.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Zero quantified water-quality PUB results reported in the survey
tier3_unverified.nBasins: unknown — no water quality PUB study with a reported site count is given

tier3_unverified.claim: REGIONAL POOLING BEAT LOCAL/REGIONAL SPECIALIZATION IN THE LARGEST STREAM-TEMPERATURE COMPARISON REPORTED: "regional LSTM models of stream temperature in the United States perform worse than the LSTM model built on all sites in the CONUS for 15 out of 17 regions" (Willard 2023). Companion negative result on the same theme: Wang et al. (2022) "show that localizing an LSTM predicting continental-scale snowpack dynamics to individual regions across the United States had insignificant benefits over the continental-scale LSTM." IMPLICATION AND CAVEAT FOR US: this is evidence AGAINST spending effort on region-specific or cluster-specific models, and FOR one pooled model over all sites — which is what we already do. But it is NOT evidence that pooling rescues between-site level prediction, and both results come from national-scale pools of hundreds-to-thousands of sites. At n=19 families confined to a single flat agricultural state, we have no "other regions" to pool with, so the mechanism that produced these gains (heterogeneous multi-region data) is structurally unavailable to us unless we expand the site pool beyond Iowa.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Pooled CONUS model beat region-specific models in 15/17 regions; regional localization of snowpack LSTM gave "insignificant benefits"
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: unknown — the 15-of-17 comparison's held-out design is not specified in the survey text; likely includes held-out sites but cannot be confirmed
tier3_unverified.nBasins: unknown site count; 17 CONUS regions for stream temperature; snowpack study is CONUS-scale

tier3_unverified.claim: THE SURVEY EXPLICITLY REJECTS THE FUNCTIONAL-SIMILARITY / DONOR-CATCHMENT PREMISE that underlies classical regionalization: entity-aware models that simply concatenate static site characteristics to dynamic inputs "challenge a longstanding hydrological perspective that transferring models and knowledge from one basin to another requires that they must be functionally similar," and the authors state "site characteristics can contain sufficient information to differentiate between site-specific dynamic behaviors for a variety of prediction tasks." FALSIFIABLE FOR US: the survey's position is that the winning strategy is NOT donor-catchment selection or similarity-index transfer but attribute concatenation inside one pooled model. Our architecture already does exactly this (lat, lon, log_basin_area, mean/max_dist_to_sensor concatenated to dynamic weather). The survey therefore predicts that our remaining between-site deficit (between_r2 0.21) is an ATTRIBUTE-COVERAGE problem — we lack the static descriptors that distinguish basins (tile drainage density being the obvious missing one) — not an architecture or transfer-method problem. This is a testable prediction: adding discriminative static attributes should move between_r2; switching to donor-transfer or similarity-weighted regionalization should not.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Qualitative/directional; no head-to-head effect size given between attribute-concatenation and donor-transfer
tier3_unverified.nBasins: claim generalized by authors from CAMELS-scale work (531 catchments) and 305-lake studies

tier3_unverified.claim: NEGATIVE RESULT ON TRANSFER FROM DATA-RICH TO DATA-POOR REGIONS: "Le et al. (2022) transfer ML streamflow models built on North America to data-poor South Africa and Central Asian regions and find that the LOCAL models trained on MINIMAL DATA OUTPERFORM the models from data-rich regions." Second relevant negative from the survey: for hybrid modeling, "the output from the NWM actually impairs the model and prevents it from learning generalizable hydrological relationships." IMPLICATION FOR US: cross-region transfer learning (e.g. pre-training on CAMELS or a national nitrate corpus and fine-tuning on Iowa) has a documented failure mode where the small local dataset wins — this directly contradicts the naive "borrow strength from 531 basins" recommendation and is the single most relevant published caution for an n=19 project considering importing an external large-sample model. It does NOT say local wins always; it says the direction is not guaranteed and must be measured, so any transfer-learning proposal here needs a local-only baseline run under the same LOFO protocol.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Local minimal-data models outperformed transferred data-rich-region models (direction reported; magnitude not given in survey)
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: unknown — cross-region transfer evaluation; held-out geography by construction (target regions unseen in training), but the internal split is not specified
tier3_unverified.nBasins: unknown — North America source pool and South Africa / Central Asia target regions; counts not given in the survey

tier3_unverified.claim: THE FIELD'S STANDARD PUB EVALUATION PROTOCOL, as defined by the survey: models "are often tested on PSEUDO UNMONITORED SITES, where data is withheld until the testing stage to mimic model building for real unmonitored sites." This is exactly our LOFO design and confirms our protocol is the field-standard one, so our 0.820 AUC is a protocol-legitimate number. IMPORTANT ABSENCE, hunted for explicitly: the survey does NOT warn about spatial autocorrelation leakage between nested or adjacent held-out sites, and does NOT prescribe grouping hydrologically nested basins into families. Our stricter leave-one-basin-FAMILY-out grouping is therefore MORE conservative than the published norm — which means (a) our numbers are likely pessimistic relative to papers reporting plain leave-one-site-out, and (b) published pseudo-unmonitored results from studies that held out individual nested sites may be optimistically biased and are not strictly comparable to our 0.820. Also note the survey reports no consensus benchmark metric or threshold for "acceptable" unmonitored-site skill.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Protocol definition, not a performance number; no consensus acceptability threshold reported
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout (pseudo-unmonitored sites; site-level withholding, nesting/grouping not specified as standard)
tier3_unverified.nBasins: varies by study; CAMELS 531 catchments is the dominant benchmark, 305 lakes for lake temperature

tier3_unverified.claim: Pandit et al. (2025) trained an LSTM on high-frequency nitrate sensor data across the conterminous US to predict DAILY NITRATE CONCENTRATION, and report a median KGE of 0.60 under temporal validation but a median KGE of only 0.18 under spatial validation (prediction in unmonitored basins). The ~0.42 KGE drop is a direct, same-paper, same-model measurement of the ungauged-basin penalty for a nitrate CONCENTRATION signal — the exact quantity our LOFO protocol measures. This is verified from the published abstract.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: median KGE 0.60 (temporal validation) vs 0.18 (spatial validation / unmonitored basins); drop of ~0.42 KGE. KGE=0.18 is barely above the mean-flow benchmark and would be considered unusable for absolute-level prediction.
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: both — the paper reports temporal-holdout AND spatial-holdout numbers separately and explicitly labels them
tier3_unverified.nBasins: unknown — the abstract says only 'high-frequency sensor data across the conterminous US'. One search snippet asserted 95 CONUS nitrate sensor sites, but this could NOT be verified against the paywalled full text. Treat 95 as unconfirmed. Order of magnitude is tens-to-low-hundreds of sites, i.e. the SAME regime as our 85 sites / 19 families, not the CAMELS 531-671 regime.

tier3_unverified.claim: In the same paper, restricting the model's application domain from all of CONUS to the Mississippi River Basin raised spatial-validation (unmonitored-basin) median KGE for nitrate concentration from 0.18 to 0.34 — roughly a doubling — without changing the model. The authors attribute this to the MRB subset having catchment attributes more similar to the training sites. This is evidence that ATTRIBUTE-SPACE / DOMAIN RESTRICTION, not more donors, is what buys ungauged-basin skill, and it directly supports our Iowa-only, agriculturally homogeneous scope being an advantage rather than a limitation.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: median KGE 0.18 (CONUS-wide spatial validation) -> 0.34 (MRB-restricted spatial validation); +0.16 KGE, ~89% relative improvement, from domain restriction alone
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout (prediction in unmonitored basins, model applied to basins not in training)
tier3_unverified.nBasins: unknown for the MRB subset; the paper notes the MRB contains 818 HUC-8s but that only a subset share attributes with the training sites. Number of held-out basins behind the 0.34 median is not determinable from available material.

tier3_unverified.claim: Shapley-value interpretation of the spatially-validated nitrate model identified TILE DRAINAGE density, ROADWAY density, and WETLAND COVER as the key spatial drivers of MEAN nitrate concentration (i.e. the between-site level, not the temporal signal), with quantitative non-linear thresholds — the paper illustrates counterfactuals such as reducing tile drain density from 60% to 0% and doubling wetland cover from 5% to 10%. This is a peer-reviewed, continental-scale confirmation that tile drainage is a first-order BETWEEN-SITE control and that its absence from our 68-feature set is a plausible primary cause of our between_r2 = 0.21 deficit. Note their tile-drainage layer is a CONUS-wide gridded product (source not identifiable from the paywalled text) — identifying it is a concrete follow-up, since we have no tile-drainage source.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: no scalar effect size available from abstract/snippets; the claim is a RANKING (tile drainage, roadway density, wetland cover as top spatial drivers of mean concentration) plus the existence of non-linear thresholds. Exact Shapley magnitudes are in the paywalled figures.
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: not-applicable (interpretation of a fitted model, though the model interpreted was the spatially-validated one)
tier3_unverified.nBasins: unknown

tier3_unverified.claim: The paper's temporal-validation protocol was 5-fold cross-validation in which 80% of each site's time series was used for training and a DIFFERENT 20% window of the SAME site's time series was held out for testing — the site's own history is in the training set. Its spatial protocol held out entire basins. Because the identical architecture scored KGE 0.60 under the first and 0.18 under the second, this paper is a clean, citable demonstration that within-site temporal holdout and spatial holdout are NOT interchangeable protocols for nitrate, and that any literature number reported without a stated protocol must be assumed to be the optimistic (temporal/random) one.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: same model, same hyperparameters, two protocols: KGE 0.60 vs 0.18. Protocol choice alone accounts for a 3.3x difference in reported skill.
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: both protocols described (temporal-holdout: 5-fold, 80/20 within-site time-series split; spatial-holdout: entire unmonitored basins)
tier3_unverified.nBasins: unknown

tier3_unverified.claim: Pandit et al. state that of the 818 HUC-8 units in the Mississippi River Basin, only a subset have catchment attributes similar to the sites used in LSTM training, and that TRANSFORMATION-BASED DOMAIN ADAPTATION was required to maintain consistency in model transfer. This is an explicit admission that a sensor-network-scale training pool does not cover the attribute space of the prediction domain, and that unrestricted extrapolation to arbitrary ungauged basins was NOT considered defensible — a direct caution for our deployment target of an ARBITRARY map pin anywhere in Iowa, where an equivalent attribute-space in-hull check does not currently exist.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: qualitative: only a subset of 818 MRB HUC-8s were deemed attribute-similar enough for transfer; exact fraction not determinable from available material
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 818 HUC-8s in the target prediction domain; number of training sites unknown

tier3_unverified.claim: The study modeled STREAMFLOW and NITRATE CONCENTRATION as two separate LSTMs, implying the nitrate pathway relies on discharge (observed or LSTM-predicted) as an input or as a companion for export computation. If the nitrate model consumes discharge, its KGE 0.18 spatial result is an OPTIMISTIC bound for our setting, because we have discharge at only 22 of 85 sites and ZERO at the 61 IWQIS sites, and our deployment target has no gauge at all. Any attempt to replicate their approach requires first building an ungauged-basin streamflow model for Iowa — an additional PUB problem stacked on top of the nitrate one.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: no direct effect size; structural claim about the modeling chain. The dependency itself is the finding.
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: unknown for the streamflow model specifically; the nitrate results are reported under both temporal-holdout and spatial-holdout
tier3_unverified.nBasins: unknown

tier3_unverified.claim: Gorski et al. (2024) predicted 7-day backward-looking average stream nitrate CONCENTRATION at 46 predominantly agricultural sites in the midwestern and eastern US using LSTMs, and DISCHARGE was a required daily dynamic input alongside meteorology plus static watershed attributes (anthropogenic hydrologic modification, N application, climate, groundwater, land use, physiography, soils). The paper's headline conclusion is that 'discharge and watershed soil and physiographic attributes showed a strong influence on model performance.' Directly relevant to our deployment target: the top-performing driver is exactly the variable we do NOT have at an arbitrary map pin (discharge is available at only 22 of our 85 sites and zero at the ungauged target), so this paper's skill level is NOT achievable by a discharge-free virtual sensor.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: qualitative attribution: discharge + soil/physiographic attributes dominate model performance

tier3_unverified.claim: Single-site LSTM models (one model trained and tested per site, 46 models) achieved a MEDIAN Kling-Gupta Efficiency of 0.66 for 7-day mean nitrate concentration. This is a per-site temporal holdout at MONITORED sites with local nitrate history, so it is an upper bound that is NOT comparable to our LOFO spatial-transfer numbers and is unattainable at an unmonitored pin by construction.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: median KGE = 0.66 (single-site models)

tier3_unverified.claim: The study compared four pooling schemes for the same 46 sites: (a) 46 single-site models, (b) 5 CLUSTERED models grouped by basin attributes, (c) 8 HYDRO TERRANE models grouped by glacial hydrogeologic terrane, and (d) 1 GLOBAL model pooling all 46 sites. Counting how often each scheme was the best model at a site: single-site best at 16 sites, hydro terrane best at 13, global best at 10, clustered best at only 7. No scheme dominated; the spread across four regionalization families is roughly 7-16 out of 46 sites, i.e. a weak and site-dependent effect rather than a decisive win for any pooling strategy.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: best-model site counts: single-site 16, hydro-terrane 13, global 10, clustered 5-group 7 (of 46)

tier3_unverified.claim: The 8 hydro-terrane group models (grouping by glacial hydrogeologic terrane, i.e. an attribute-similarity regionalization) achieved median KGE = 0.65 and median RMSE = 1.03 mg/L, and produced only ONE site with KGE < 0 - the fewest catastrophic failures of any of the four schemes. This is the paper's strongest evidence that attribute-based grouping buys ROBUSTNESS (fewer blow-ups on odd basins) rather than higher median skill: median KGE 0.65 vs 0.66 for single-site models is essentially a wash.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: median KGE 0.65, median RMSE 1.03 mg/L, 1 site with KGE<0 (vs more for other schemes); median KGE within 0.01 of single-site 0.66
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 46 sites in 8 terrane groups

tier3_unverified.claim: NEGATIVE RESULT, explicitly stated in the abstract: 'Developing a single model for all sites reduced performance at several locations with distinct characteristics, suggesting that there is a threshold of dissimilarity beyond which more data does not improve the model.' The authors further state: 'While many deep learning studies have shown that national or even global models can outperform local models, it is not clear that this is true for water quality constituents.' This contradicts the streamflow-PUB literature (CAMELS-scale regional LSTMs beating local models) and warns that the well-known 'pool more basins, get more skill' scaling law observed at n=531-671 streamflow catchments does NOT demonstrably hold for nitrate concentration at n=46.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: global all-site pooling DEGRADED performance at several distinct-character sites; global model was best at only 10 of 46 sites

tier3_unverified.claim: This paper reports NO leave-one-site-out / spatially-held-out (ungauged-basin) evaluation and NO between-site R2 of site mean nitrate. Every reported number is per-site performance at sites that contributed training data, so the paper supplies zero direct evidence on the between-basin transfer problem that is our entire remaining headroom. Its usable transfer signal is indirect: grouping sites by physical/hydrogeologic attributes (5-8 groups over 46 sites, i.e. ~6-9 sites per group - comparable in scale to our 19 basin families) improved the WORST sites, implying that at small n the realistic gain from attribute-based regionalization is failure-mode reduction on atypical basins, not a lift in median skill.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: no spatial-holdout number reported; no between-site R2 reported
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 46 sites; groups of 5 (attribute clusters) and 8 (hydro terranes)

tier3_unverified.claim: PRIMARY SOURCE IS PAYWALLED. Oudin et al. (2008), WRR 44(3), DOI 10.1029/2007WR006240, returned HTTP 403 on both the Wiley full-text HTML and the 'bronze OA' pdfdirect link; Semantic Scholar reports the publisher elided the abstract from metadata (551 citations). From abstract mirrors and secondary citation, the paper's RANKING of regionalization families over 913 French catchments using two lumped daily rainfall-runoff models is: spatial proximity BEST, physical similarity INTERMEDIATE, regression-on-attributes WORST -- with the explicit statement that regression results were 'very close to those obtained using one median parameter set for the whole country', i.e. attribute regression added essentially ZERO skill over a single global constant parameter set. Exact NSE values per method could NOT be recovered and remain unverified. Directly relevant verdict for our project: in a country with a DENSE gauge network, plain geographic proximity beat attribute-based similarity -- consistent with lat/lon already being our #2 and #3 features, and predicting that adding more static physical attributes as regression inputs will underperform simple proximity.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Qualitative ranking only: spatial proximity > physical similarity > regression ~= single national median parameter set. No numeric NSE recoverable from accessible sources.
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: unknown - could not be determined from accessible metadata; secondary sources imply each catchment treated as ungauged in turn (spatial holdout), but this is NOT confirmed and the exact donor-exclusion rule is unverified
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 913 French catchments

tier3_unverified.claim: THE DONOR-COUNT SCALING CURVE (this is the explicit curve requested, from a substitute source I could read in full): Patil & Stieglitz (2012, HESS 16:551-562, doi:10.5194/hess-16-551-2012), 756 US HCDN catchments, each treated as ungauged in turn (jack-knife), inverse-distance-weighted transfer of area-normalized daily streamflow from N nearest gauged neighbors, N swept 1 to 50. Median Nash-Sutcliffe rises SHARPLY from 0.49 at N=1 to 0.61 at N=4, then only marginally to a maximum of 0.615 at N=15, and DECLINES beyond 15 donors. The curve is essentially FLAT from N=4 onward. Falsifiable implication for our n=19-basin-families constraint: the marginal value of donor catchments saturates at roughly 4-5 donors, so having only 19 independent families is NOT obviously fatal for proximity-style donor transfer -- the published gain from 19 donors to 500 donors is near zero on this curve. This is the single most important number for assessing our sample-size constraint, and it argues the n=19 limit is far less binding for DONOR-TRANSFER methods than for methods that learn a global attribute->level regression.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Median NS: 0.49 (N=1 donor) -> 0.61 (N=4) -> 0.615 max (N=15) -> declining beyond N=15. Gain from 1 to 4 donors = +0.12 NS; gain from 4 to 15 donors = +0.005 NS.
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout (jack-knife: each of the 756 catchments held out and treated as ungauged in turn; predictions built only from OTHER catchments' observed streamflow)
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 756 (continental US, HCDN, drainage area 23-5000 km2, median 715 km2, WY1970-1988)

tier3_unverified.claim: NEGATIVE RESULT, DIRECTLY CONTRADICTING THE INTUITION THAT MORE NEARBY MONITORING HELPS: in Patil & Stieglitz (2012), gauge density around an ungauged catchment (number of gauged catchments within a 200 km radius) had NO significant relationship with prediction skill. Among catchments with NS > 0, the R2 between NS and gauge density is 0.06 -- density of surrounding gauges explains only 6% of the spatial variability in NS. The result was robust to varying the search radius from 100 km to 500 km. Verbatim: 'Contrary to our a priori expectation, high gauge density around an ungauged catchment does not guarantee good predictability. Moreover, there are numerous catchments that have low gauge density in their vicinity and still have high NS values.' Implication for us: proposals to improve between-site skill by weighting or borrowing from denser clusters of Iowa sensors have a published prior of failure; and conversely, our 19-family sparsity is not by itself the reason between_r2 is 0.21.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: R2 = 0.06 between NS and gauge density within 200 km; no significant trend; robust to 100-500 km radii.

tier3_unverified.claim: SPATIAL PROXIMITY ITSELF EXPLAINS ONLY 12% OF TRANSFER SKILL. In Patil & Stieglitz (2012), among catchments with NS > 0, the R2 between NS and average distance to donor catchments is 0.12; Spearman rho of NS with average donor distance is -0.44 and with nearest-donor distance -0.41 (both p < 0.01), but the authors note 'a surprisingly wide scatter of distances between donor and receiver catchments' at any given NS, concluding 'the donor-receiver catchment proximity alone cannot fully explain the prediction performance at a given location.' Falsifiable implication: even in the best-performing regionalization family (proximity), the achievable between-site skill is bounded -- distance is a real but weak signal (rho ~ -0.4), which is quantitatively similar in magnitude to our own between_r2 of 0.21 / between_rate_r2 of 0.24. This suggests our between-site deficit may be near the published PUB ceiling rather than a fixable feature-engineering gap.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: R2 = 0.12 (NS vs average donor distance); Spearman rho = -0.44 (average distance), -0.41 (nearest-donor distance), p < 0.01.

tier3_unverified.claim: THE ATTRIBUTES THAT PREDICT TRANSFERABILITY ARE HYDROLOGIC SIGNATURES YOU CANNOT COMPUTE AT AN UNGAUGED PIN -- STATIC PHYSIOGRAPHY IS NEARLY USELESS. Patil & Stieglitz (2012) correlated 8 catchment properties against ungauged-prediction NS across 756 catchments (Table 1, Spearman rho): PHYSIOGRAPHIC (available at an ungauged pin) -- channel slope 0.21 (p=0.00), soil permeability 0.08 (p=0.03), soil water holding capacity 0.04 (p=0.26, NOT significant); HYDROLOGIC SIGNATURES (require an existing gauge record) -- runoff ratio 0.51 (p=0.00), baseflow runoff ratio 0.46 (p=0.00), slope of flow duration curve 0.31 (p=0.00), baseflow index 0.03 (p=0.46, NOT significant), inter-annual streamflow elasticity 0.01 (p=0.83, NOT significant). Only 4 of 8 properties were significant and the authors call the relationships 'weak', stating attribute analysis 'provides, at best, a weak picture of the physiographic and hydro-climatic conditions that favor high streamflow similarity.' For our deployment target (arbitrary map pin, no local history) the ONLY usable attributes -- slope, permeability, SWHC -- have rho of 0.21, 0.08, 0.04. This is direct published evidence AGAINST the hypothesis that a richer static-attribute feature set will close our between-site gap.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Usable-at-ungauged-pin attributes: channel slope rho=0.21, permeability rho=0.08, SWHC rho=0.04 (n.s.). Gauge-requiring signatures: runoff ratio rho=0.51, baseflow runoff ratio rho=0.46, FDC slope rho=0.31.

tier3_unverified.claim: FLAT TERRAIN IS A PUBLISHED PREDICTOR OF MEDIOCRE UNGAUGED SKILL -- BAD NEWS FOR IOWA SPECIFICALLY. Patil & Stieglitz (2012) partitioned 756 US catchments into Group 1 (NS>0.7, 288 catchments, ~40%), Group 2 (0.3<NS<0.7, 277, ~35%), Group 3 (NS<0.3, 191, ~25%, described as 'practically unpredictable using our spatial proximity based prediction method'). High-predictability catchments are 'confined to the Appalachian Mountains in eastern US, the Rocky Mountains, and the Cascade Mountains in the Pacific Northwest.' The authors explicitly test the flat-but-humid case: 'the catchments in southeastern states of Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama and Florida have humid climate, but a flatter terrain (and most are Group 2 catchments)', concluding 'climate alone does not appear to be sufficient... topography is also an important factor in determining streamflow similarity.' At 5 donors the overall distribution is median NS 0.61, 25th percentile 0.29, maximum 0.97. Note the paper does place SOME Group 1 catchments in Indiana and Illinois. Implication: for flat agricultural Midwest terrain the published expectation for proximity-based ungauged transfer is Group-2-like performance, not Group 1 -- our LOFO AUC 0.820 / between_r2 0.21 is plausibly at the regional ceiling for this landscape class.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: At 5 donors: median NS 0.61, 25th pct 0.29, max 0.97. 25% of catchments effectively unpredictable (NS<0.3). Flat humid southeast = predominantly Group 2 despite humid climate.
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout (leave-one-catchment-out jack-knife, 5 donor catchments, IDW p=2)

tier3_unverified.claim: Oudin et al. (2010) tested directly whether physically similar catchments are hydrologically similar, using 893 French + 10 English catchments (903 total). Verbatim from the abstract: "The results show that the overlap between the two pools is significant for only 60% of the catchments." I.e. for ~40% of catchments, the pool of catchments selected as most physically similar (via physiographic descriptors) has NO significant overlap with the pool that is empirically hydrologically similar (defined by which donors' model parameters actually transfer successfully). This is the canonical falsification of the core assumption behind attribute-based regionalization. RELEVANCE TO US: our per-basin static attributes (crop fractions, N-surplus, area, mean/max distance) are exactly this kind of physiographic descriptor set, and this result predicts they will identify the right hydrologic analogue for only ~60% of unseen basins.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Overlap between apparent-similarity and behavioral-similarity pools significant for only 60% of catchments (40% failure rate).
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout — behavioral similarity is defined by transferring calibrated model parameter sets between catchment pairs, i.e. each catchment is treated as hypothetically ungauged and scored on donors' parameters. Note this is a pool-overlap analysis, not a single held-out skill score; no NSE table could be retrieved because the paper is paywalled.
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 903 (893 French + 10 English); the 893 figure is confirmed in the open-access HESS 2011 review, which states Oudin et al. (2010) used "893 French and 10 English catchments"

tier3_unverified.claim: Oudin et al. (2010) identify a SPECIFIC cause of the attribute-similarity failure, verbatim from the abstract: the non-overlapping catchments failed because "(1) these catchments often have a quite specific hydrological behavior and (2) the role of the underground properties of the catchment on its hydrological behavior was not found to be accurately described by the available physical descriptors, meaning that more relevant catchment descriptors should be sought to better describe the geological and lithological context in hydrological terms." DIRECT IMPLICATION FOR THIS PROJECT: the diagnosed missing information is SUBSURFACE, not surface land use or weather. In an Iowa nitrate context the analogous missing subsurface control is tile drainage density / subsurface hydraulic connectivity — which this project has already flagged as the dominant Iowa control and absent from the feature set. This is independent literature support for prioritizing a subsurface-drainage covariate over any further weather feature engineering.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Qualitative diagnosis, no number attached; explains the 40% non-overlap in the claim above.

tier3_unverified.claim: The companion study Oudin et al. (2008), 913 French catchments, ranks regionalization families head-to-head. Verbatim from the abstract: "in France, where a dense network of gauging stations is available, spatial proximity provides the best regionalization solution. The regression approach is the least satisfactory, with results very close to those obtained using one median parameter set for the whole country. The physical similarity approach is intermediary. However, the results obtained with these three methods lag far behind those obtained by full model calibration. Our results also show that some improvement could be made by combining spatial proximity and physical similarity." RANKING: spatial proximity > physical similarity > regression-on-attributes ~= a single national constant. RELEVANCE: this is direct evidence that lat/lon (spatial proximity) already being top-3 in our feature importance is the EXPECTED outcome, not an anomaly, and that adding more catchment-attribute regressors is the family with the WEAKEST published payoff. Caveat: the abstract explicitly conditions the proximity win on a DENSE gauge network; no per-method NSE values could be extracted because the paper is paywalled.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Ordinal ranking only from the abstract (proximity > similarity > regression ≈ national median parameter set); all three 'lag far behind' full local calibration. Exact NSE values not retrievable.
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout — ungauged-basin protocol, each catchment treated as ungauged and predicted from other catchments' parameters
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 913 French catchments, two lumped rainfall-runoff models (daily)

tier3_unverified.claim: Pool et al. (2021), 671 CAMELS catchments (contiguous US), leave-one-out cross-validation, HBV-light, 23 regionalization methods — the largest homogenized comparison available. Median RNP (Nash-type relative performance): local calibration (upper benchmark) 0.89; best-available-donor 0.87; distance+volume combined 0.82; volume/signature-based 0.80; spatial proximity alone 0.79; CATCHMENT ATTRIBUTES alone 0.78; fixed catchment classification 0.76; RANDOM donor 0.69-0.70. Verbatim: "we found that distance-based approaches tend to outperform attribute-based approaches." NOTE THE EFFECT SIZES: the entire spread from random donor (0.69) to the best method (0.82) is 0.13 RNP, and the spread between spatial proximity (0.79) and attribute similarity (0.78) is 0.01 — i.e. choosing attribute-similarity over proximity buys essentially NOTHING even with 670 donors available. VERDICT ON THE RESEARCH QUESTION: attribute-based similarity does NOT beat plain spatial proximity, and the authors attribute the proximity win partly to high gauge density and partly to "the lack of catchment attributes representing a wide range of catchment responses over large scales (Merz et al., 2020; Oudin et al., 2010)."
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Median RNP: local calib 0.89 / best donor 0.87 / dist+volume 0.82 / volume 0.80 / distance 0.79 / attributes 0.78 / classification 0.76 / random 0.69. Attribute-vs-proximity gap = 0.01 RNP. Full method spread = 0.13 RNP.
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout — explicit leave-one-out cross-validation with the receiver catchment treated as ungauged
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 671 CAMELS catchments

tier3_unverified.claim: Pool et al. (2021) quantify DONOR SCARCITY directly, and this is the single most important number against the n=19-families constraint. With all 671 CAMELS catchments calibrated and each of the other 670 tested as a donor: "For a relative performance value of 0.7, half of the hypothetically ungauged catchments have at most 23 suitable donor catchments" — i.e. only ~3.4% of 670 candidate donors are usable at that threshold. Further: "at least three potential donors exist for 85% of the hypothetically ungauged catchments" at that threshold, and at a 0.9 threshold "for 40% of the catchments, only one donor exceeds the performance threshold." Also verbatim: "for 50% of the hypothetically ungauged catchments, more than 40% of the donor catchments perform at least as well as randomly selected parameter sets" — meaning for the other half, MOST donors are worse than random parameters. EXTRAPOLATION TO THIS PROJECT: if only ~3.4% of donors are suitable, a pool of 19 independent basin families yields an EXPECTED 0.65 suitable donors per target basin — under one. Any donor-transfer or nearest-analogue regionalization scheme is therefore very likely infeasible at n=19, and this paper's own numbers are the evidence, not an assertion. It also means the observed between_r2 of 0.21 may be near the structural ceiling for donor-style transfer at this sample size.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: At relative performance 0.7: median catchment has ≤23 suitable donors out of 670 (3.4%). At 0.9: 40% of catchments have exactly one suitable donor. For 50% of catchments, >60% of donors are worse than random parameter sets.
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout — every catchment treated as hypothetically ungauged, exhaustive all-pairs donor evaluation
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 671 (each tested against the other 670 as donors)

tier3_unverified.claim: Spatial-proximity regionalization has a GAUGE-DENSITY CLIFF, which bounds how far proximity can carry this project. Lebecherel, Andréassian & Perrin (2016, J. Hydrol. 539:196) deliberately degraded the French hydrometric network using a 'hydrometrical desert' protocol (progressively deleting the CLOSEST gauged stations to the target, which they argue is more realistic than random deletion). Reported result: performance of spatial-proximity output-averaging methods deteriorates strongly once station density falls below roughly 0.6 gauges per 1000 km2. ARITHMETIC FOR IOWA: 85 sensor sites over ~145,746 km2 = 0.58 gauges per 1000 km2 — AT the reported cliff. Using the leak-safe count of 19 independent basin families instead gives 0.13 per 1000 km2, roughly 4.5x BELOW the cliff. This predicts that lat/lon proximity, already top-3 in our permutation importance, is operating near or past the density at which proximity-based transfer degrades, and that further squeezing the proximity family has limited headroom. CAVEAT: the 0.6 threshold was obtained from a secondary summary of the paper, not from the full text, which is paywalled at Elsevier; treat the exact threshold value as unverified, though the qualitative density dependence is corroborated by Oudin et al. (2008)'s own conditioning of its proximity result on 'a dense network of gauging stations.'
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Spatial-proximity performance 'strongly deteriorates' below ~0.6 gauging stations per 1000 km2 (threshold value unverified from primary text). Iowa equivalent: 0.58/1000 km2 at 85 sites; 0.13/1000 km2 at 19 independent families.
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: spatial-holdout — ungauged-basin protocol with deliberate network degradation ('hydrometrical desert', deleting nearest gauges)
tier3_unverified.nBasins: French national dataset (same family as the 913-catchment Oudin set); exact retained count not verified from full text
